lesson.title: The Blueprint: What a Class Really Is
lesson.summary: A class is a blueprint that defines what data and behavior every object built from it will share, without itself being any single one of those objects.
lesson.body:
In the object-oriented programming overview, the plan was to bundle a dog's data and behavior together into one object. But before Python can build even one dog object, it needs to know what a dog object is supposed to look like: what information it holds, and what it can do. That description is called a class. A class does not represent one specific dog, the way rex or fido might; it represents the general shape that every dog object will follow, similar to how a blueprint for a house is not itself a house you can live in, it is the plan that every house built from it will follow.

In Python, you create a class with the class keyword, followed by a name, written in PascalCase (each word capitalized, no underscores) by convention, to visually distinguish class names from variable and function names.

```python
class Dog:
    """A blueprint describing what every dog object will have."""
    pass

print(type(Dog))
print(Dog)
```

```
<class 'type'>
<class '__main__.Dog'>
```

The pass statement is a placeholder meaning "this class body is empty for now," the same role it plays in an empty function or loop. Notice what printing type(Dog) reveals: Dog itself is a value in Python, and its type is type, meaning classes themselves are objects too, specifically objects that describe how to build other objects. Printing Dog directly shows <class '__main__.Dog'>, confirming it is a class defined in this file (the module Python calls __main__ when you run a script directly), not yet an actual dog.

This distinction between the blueprint and the things built from it, between the class and its objects, is the foundation for everything else in object-oriented programming. The next concept looks at what happens on the other side of that blueprint: the actual objects a class produces.
